newsitem.title: USA: Airline stocks jump, led by UAL.
newsitem.headline: Airline stocks jump, led by UAL.

text.p: The stocks of U.S. airlines jumped on Tuesday after UAL Corp. forecast that its first-quarter earnings would exceed Wall Street estimates.
The bullish forecast from UAL, the parent company of United Airlines, set an upbeat tone for the rest of the sector, analysts said.

Carriers have benefited from the lapse of the passenger excise tax and labour disruption at AMR Corp.'s American Airlines, analysts said. First-quarter revenues and load factors will likely be stronger than year-ago results.

UAL said it expects first-quarter earnings to exceed the highest estimate of those given by analysts surveyed by First Call, which was $1.30 a share. UAL earned 77 cents a share in the year-ago quarter. United said February traffic, combined with January results, have led it to re-evaluate its outlook for the first quarter.

UAL's stock jumped $4.25 to $64.125 in late trading on the New York Stock Exchange, with Delta Air Lines Inc. up $1.375 at $83.625 and Continental Airlines Inc. gaining 62.5 cents to $29.625. But AMR was off 12.5 cents at $80.625, also on the NYSE.
The Dow Jones transport index was up more than 27 points to 2,400.
The threat of a strike by American Air pilots created a first-quarter windfall for rival carriers, especially United. Passengers shied away from American as the Feb. 15 strike deadline loomed.

"Some airlines benefited from the disruptions at American. United and American share a hub in Chicago, so United got a boost for about a week to 10 days," said Jeffrey Long, an analyst with J.P. Morgan.
Continental and Delta also absorbed additional travelers and "good will" during American's labour problems, analysts said.
President Clinton imposed a cooling-off period on American and its pilots, preventing a strike, and travelers were later wooed back to the carrier by deep fare discounts.
Airlines also benefited in the first quarter from the lapsed passenger excise tax.
"The airlines are getting a better boost from the excise tax this year," said Brian Harris, an analyst with Lehman Brothers.
Airlines have culled extra revenues since Jan. 1 by pocketing the 10 percent tax that would normally go to the federal government. The tax is expected to be reinstated within the next two weeks.
The tax was absent last year as well. Airlines initially passed on the savings to consumers, but then slowly raised fares throughout the year.
This year, airlines are keeping the extra money for themselves.
Carriers may try to raise fares when the tax is reinstated. If consumers balk, carriers may have to increase fares more slowly, analysts said.
